results.title: Confidence Intervals: Finding Certainty in Uncertainty | by Jani Data Diaries | Medium
results.content: # Confidence Intervals: Finding Certainty in Uncertainty. In statistics, this concept is called a **Confidence Interval (CI)**. Rather than pinpointing an exact number, confidence intervals provide a range that reflects the uncertainty in your estimates. Let’s dive into the world of confidence intervals and see how they guide decision-making, just like a treasure map. ## Step 1: What is a Confidence Interval? A confidence interval is a range of values derived from sample data. It is used to estimate a population parameter with a specified level of confidence, usually 95% or 99%. The width of the interval reflects the uncertainty in your estimate. 1. **Point Estimate**: The center of the interval (e.g., sample mean). 3. **Confidence Level**: Indicates how confident you are that the interval contains the true value (e.g., 95%). ## Step 2: Why Do We Use Confidence Intervals? 2. **Quantify Precision**: Narrower intervals indicate more precise estimates. A precise map with a narrow range gives you more confidence to start digging. ## Step 3: Calculating a Confidence Interval. The team calculates that the ship is likely 500 meters below the surface, with a confidence interval of 500±50 meters. With this interval, the team decides where to focus their efforts, understanding the margin of error reflects the variability in their data. Here’s how to calculate a confidence interval for a sample mean:. import numpy as npfrom scipy.stats import norm# Sample datadata = [10, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 21]sample_mean = np.mean(data)sample_std = np.std(data, ddof=1)sample_size = len(data)confidence_level = 0.95# Z-score for 95% confidence levelz_score = norm.ppf(1 - (1 - confidence_level) / 2)# Margin of Errormargin_of_error = z_score * (sample_std / np.sqrt(sample_size))# Confidence Intervallower_bound = sample_mean - margin_of_errorupper_bound = sample_mean + margin_of_errorprint(f"Confidence Interval: ({lower_bound:.2f}, {upper_bound:.2f})"). **Story**: Imagine a pharmaceutical company using a confidence interval to predict the effectiveness of a vaccine. ## Step 7: Challenges with Confidence Intervals. 2. **Misinterpretation**: A 95% CI doesn’t mean there’s a 95% chance the true value is inside — it means 95% of intervals constructed this way will contain the true value. Confidence intervals are like treasure maps in the world of data. Whether you’re a scientist, business analyst, or engineer, mastering confidence intervals equips you with a powerful tool to navigate uncertainty.

results.content:
Title: Trajectory planning under environmental uncertainty with finite-sample safety guarantees - ScienceDirect
## Automatica. Volume 131, September 2021, 109754. # Brief paper Trajectory planning under environmental uncertainty with finite-sample safety guarantees☆. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.automatica.2021.109754Get rights and content. We tackle the problem of trajectory planning in an environment comprised of a set of obstacles with uncertain time-varying locations. The uncertainties are modeled using widely accepted Gaussian distributions, resulting in a chance-constrained program. Contrary to previous approaches however, we do not assume perfect knowledge of the moments of the distribution, and instead estimate them through finite samples available from either sensors or past data. We derive tight concentration bounds on the error of these estimates to sufficiently tighten the chance-constraint program. As such, we provide provable guarantees on satisfaction of the chance-constraints corresponding to the nominal yet unknown moments. We illustrate our results with two autonomous vehicle trajectory planning case studies. **Vasileios Lefkopoulos** holds an M.Sc. degree in Robotics, Systems and Control from ETH Zurich, Switzerland, and a Diploma degree in Electrical and Computer Engineering from the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki, Greece. His research interests include model predictive control and optimal control theory with applications in trajectory planning and control of autonomous systems. **Maryam Kamgarpour** is with the faculty of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of British Columbia, Vancouver, Canada. She holds a Doctor of Philosophy in Engineering from the University of California, Berkeley and a Bachelor of Applied Science from University of Waterloo, Canada. Her research is on safe decision-making and control under uncertainty, game theory and mechanism design, mixed integer and stochastic optimization and control. Her theoretical research is motivated by control challenges arising in intelligent transportation networks, robotics, power grid systems and healthcare. She is the recipient of NASA High Potential Individual Award, NASA Excellence in Publication Award, and the European Union (ERC) Starting Grant. Kamgarpour is gratefully supported by the Swiss National Science Foundation, under the grant SNSF 200021\_172782, and by the NSERC, Canada Discovery Grant RGPAS-2020-00110. The material in this paper was partially presented at the 18th European Control Conference, June 25–28, 2019, Naples, Italy. This paper was recommended for publication in revised form by Associate Editor Andrey V. Savkin under the direction of Editor Ian R.

Title: Maximum Mean Discrepancy Distributionally Robust Nonlinear Chance-Constrained Optimization with Finite-Sample Guarantee
Maximum Mean Discrepancy Distributionally Robust Nonlinear Chance-Constrained Optimization with Finite-Sample Guarantee | IEEE Conference Publication | IEEE Xplore. Image 1: IEEE Xplore logo - Link to home. Conferences>2022 IEEE 61st Conference on ... Maximum Mean Discrepancy Distributionally Robust Nonlinear Chance-Constrained Optimization with Finite-Sample Guarantee. This paper is motivated by addressing open questions in distributionally robust chance-constrained programs (DRCCP) using the popular Wasserstein ambiguity sets. This paper is motivated by addressing open questions in distributionally robust chance-constrained programs (DRCCP) using the popular Wasserstein ambiguity sets. In contrast, we propose a practical DRCCP algorithm using kernel maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) ambiguity sets, which we term MMD-DRCCP, to treat general nonlinear constraints without using ad-hoc reformulation techniques. MMD-DRCCP can handle general nonlinear and non-convex constraints with a proven finite-sample constraint satisfaction guarantee of a dimension-independent O(1 N√) rate, achievable by a practical algorithm. Our algorithm is validated numerically on a portfolio optimization problem and a tube-based distributionally robust model predictive control problem with non-convex constraints. **Published in:**2022 IEEE 61st Conference on Decision and Control (CDC). Compared to their robust optimization counterparts, CCP solutions often satisfy the constraints with high probability in practice while maintaining performance. For this reason, CCP has recently been combined with distributionally robust optimization [8] (DRO) using Wasserstein ambiguity sets [22], [11], as proposed by works such as [38], [16]. DRO addresses uncertain optimization problems by finding a solution for the worst-case distribution from a set of distributions, the ambiguity set. In this paper, we will focus on ambiguity sets constructed using Wasserstein distances, and kernel maximum mean discrepancy. Within the Wasserstein ambiguity set DRCCP framework, with the notable exceptions of [16], [15], most works limit the class of constraint functions to be affine in the uncertainty variable [38], [5], [26]. results.title: Margin of Error in Statistics
results.content: The margin of error (MOE) is a statistic expressing the amount of random sampling error in survey results or estimates derived from sample data. For example, if a political poll reports a candidate’s support at 52% with a margin of error of ±3%, it means the candidate’s true support in the entire population is likely between 49% and 55%, given the confidence level specified. The margin of error depends on the variability of the data, the size of the sample, and the confidence level. For example, if an election poll estimates 48% support with a ±3% margin of error, the confidence interval is from 45% to 51%. Recognizing the margin of error’s ties to sample size, confidence levels, and sampling methods is essential for accurate data interpretation and effective communication. A1: Margin of error is the amount added and subtracted from a sample estimate to create the confidence interval.
